---
title: "8. Cloud SQL and Firestore"
description: "Two managed databases for the Lemonade Stand: Cloud SQL Postgres for orders, Firestore for simple counters, plus connections, backups and high availability."
---

Cloud Run instances come and go, so the Lemonade Stand needs somewhere permanent to keep its data. Google Cloud offers many databases. This lesson covers the two a small app is most likely to need: **Cloud SQL**, a managed PostgreSQL server, and **Firestore**, a document database with no server at all.

## The problem

- **Orders** have a fixed shape (who, which drink, how many, when) and must never be lost or double-counted. They belong in a relational database with transactions.
- **"Cups sold today"** is one number, updated on every sale and read on every page view. A full SQL server is overkill for that.
- The owner does not want to install Postgres, patch it, or remember to take backups.

## Explain it like I'm ten

::: {.callout-tip}
**Cloud SQL** is a **tidy filing cabinet**. Every drawer is a **table**, and every sheet in it is filled in on the **same form**: name, drink, cups, time. A **twin cabinet** in another building copies every sheet the moment it is written. If the first building has a fire, the twin takes over. Every night, someone photocopies the whole cabinet: that is a **backup**.

The idea of keeping data in neat tables of rows comes from Edgar F. Codd, who described the **relational model** in 1970 in "A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks" ([Communications of the ACM](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/362384.362685)). Postgres, MySQL and Cloud SQL all follow his idea.

**Firestore** is a **box of index cards**. Each card (a **document**) can have whatever you write on it, such as `cups: 42`. Cards are grouped into folders (**collections**). There is no cabinet to look after: Google keeps the box.
:::

## The idea, precisely

### Cloud SQL

| Concept | Meaning | Lemonade value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Instance | one managed database server | `lemonade-db` |
| Edition | `enterprise` or `enterprise-plus` (faster, bigger, higher SLA) | `enterprise` |
| Tier | machine size | `db-custom-1-3840` (1 vCPU, 3.75 GB) |
| Database | a named database inside the instance | `orders` |
| Connection name | `PROJECT:REGION:INSTANCE` | `lemonade-stand-dev:europe-west2:lemonade-db` |
| Availability type | `ZONAL` (one zone) or `REGIONAL` (primary plus standby in another zone) | `REGIONAL` in prod |

**High availability** (`--availability-type=REGIONAL`) keeps a standby in a second zone, with every write copied to it before it is confirmed. If the primary's zone fails, Cloud SQL switches over automatically, usually within about a minute. Google's SLA for the Enterprise edition is 99.95% a month.

**Backups.** Automated backups run daily in a window you choose (`--backup-start-time`), and by default the last 7 are kept. **Point-in-time recovery** (`--enable-point-in-time-recovery`) also keeps the write-ahead log, so you can restore to any moment inside the log-retention window, not only to last night.

**Connecting from Cloud Run.** Add `--add-cloudsql-instances=<connection name>` to `gcloud run deploy`. Cloud Run then opens a Unix socket at `/cloudsql/<connection name>`, and the app connects to that path as its host. The service account needs `roles/cloudsql.client` (lesson 3). No public IP and no firewall rule are involved.

```js
import pg from 'pg';

export const pool = new pg.Pool({
  host: `/cloudsql/${process.env.INSTANCE_CONNECTION_NAME}`,
  database: 'orders',
  user: 'lemonade',
  password: process.env.DB_PASSWORD,
  max: 5, // at most 5 connections per Cloud Run instance
});
```

### Firestore

| Concept | Meaning | Lemonade value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Database | one per project to start, named `(default)`, in one location | `europe-west2` |
| Collection | a group of documents | `daily` |
| Document | up to 1 MiB of fields, addressed by a path | `daily/2026-11-25` |
| Field | a typed value | `cups: 42` |

Firestore needs no instance size. It scales by itself, and you pay per document read, write and delete, plus storage. The Standard edition has a daily free allowance of 50,000 reads, 20,000 writes and 20,000 deletes, and 1 GiB of storage (at the time of writing).

Counting a sale is one atomic write:

```js
import { Firestore, FieldValue } from '@google-cloud/firestore';

const db = new Firestore();
await db.doc('daily/2026-11-25').set({ cups: FieldValue.increment(1) }, { merge: true });
```

`FieldValue.increment` adds 1 on the server, so two sales at the same moment both count.

### Which one?

| Need | Choose |
| --- | --- |
| Joins, transactions across tables, SQL reports | Cloud SQL |
| Simple documents and counters, no server to size, scale to zero | Firestore |
| Both | both: they are not rivals |

## Command reference

| Command or flag | What it does | Rule / convention | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `gcloud sql instances create` | creates a Postgres server | takes several minutes | `gcloud sql instances create lemonade-db --database-version=POSTGRES_17 --edition=enterprise --tier=db-custom-1-3840 --region=europe-west2` |
| `--availability-type` | `ZONAL` or `REGIONAL` (high availability) | `REGIONAL` for prod | `--availability-type=REGIONAL` |
| `--backup-start-time` | daily backup window (UTC, `HH:MM`) | pick a quiet hour | `--backup-start-time=03:00` |
| `--enable-point-in-time-recovery` | keeps logs for any-moment restores | on for prod | `--enable-point-in-time-recovery` |
| `gcloud sql databases create` | creates a database in the instance | | `gcloud sql databases create orders --instance=lemonade-db` |
| `gcloud sql users create` | creates a database user | keep the password in Secret Manager | `gcloud sql users create lemonade --instance=lemonade-db --password="$DB_PASSWORD"` |
| `gcloud sql instances describe` | shows settings, including the connection name | | `gcloud sql instances describe lemonade-db --format="value(connectionName)"` |
| `gcloud sql connect` | opens `psql` to the instance | for admin work, not for apps | `gcloud sql connect lemonade-db --user=postgres --database=orders` |
| `gcloud sql backups create` / `list` | takes or lists backups | take one before risky changes | `gcloud sql backups create --instance=lemonade-db` |
| `gcloud sql instances patch` | changes settings | some changes restart the server | `gcloud sql instances patch lemonade-db --availability-type=REGIONAL` |
| `gcloud sql instances delete` | deletes the instance **and its automated backups** | take a final export first | `gcloud sql instances delete lemonade-db` |
| `gcloud run deploy --add-cloudsql-instances` | gives Cloud Run the socket to the instance | use the connection name | `--add-cloudsql-instances=lemonade-stand-dev:europe-west2:lemonade-db` |
| `gcloud firestore databases create` | creates the `(default)` Firestore database | the location is permanent | `gcloud firestore databases create --location=europe-west2` |
| `gcloud firestore databases list` | lists Firestore databases | | `gcloud firestore databases list` |

## Worked example: orders in Postgres, cups in Firestore

```bash
gcloud services enable sqladmin.googleapis.com firestore.googleapis.com

gcloud sql instances create lemonade-db --database-version=POSTGRES_17 --edition=enterprise \
  --tier=db-custom-1-3840 --region=europe-west2 --backup-start-time=03:00
gcloud sql databases create orders --instance=lemonade-db
gcloud sql users create lemonade --instance=lemonade-db --password="$DB_PASSWORD"

gcloud run deploy lemonade-web --image="$REGISTRY/lemonade-stand:v1" --region=europe-west2 \
  --service-account=lemonade-run@lemonade-stand-dev.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --add-cloudsql-instances=lemonade-stand-dev:europe-west2:lemonade-db \
  --set-env-vars=INSTANCE_CONNECTION_NAME=lemonade-stand-dev:europe-west2:lemonade-db \
  --max-instances=10

gcloud firestore databases create --location=europe-west2
```

Illustrative output:

```text
Creating Cloud SQL instance for POSTGRES_17...done.
Created [https://sqladmin.googleapis.com/sql/v1beta4/projects/lemonade-stand-dev/instances/lemonade-db].
NAME         DATABASE_VERSION  LOCATION        TIER              PRIMARY_ADDRESS  PRIVATE_ADDRESS  STATUS
lemonade-db  POSTGRES_17       europe-west2-b  db-custom-1-3840  192.0.2.90       -                RUNNABLE
```

(`DB_PASSWORD` came from a password manager. In production, store it in Secret Manager and pass it with `--set-secrets` instead of an environment variable you typed.)

## Rules and conventions

- Keep the database in the **same region** as Cloud Run (`europe-west2`).
- Connect from Cloud Run through `--add-cloudsql-instances` (or the Cloud SQL connectors), never through a public IP opened to `0.0.0.0/0`.
- Size the connection pool from the formula below, and always set Cloud Run's `--max-instances`.
- Production: `--availability-type=REGIONAL`, daily backups and point-in-time recovery. Dev: `ZONAL`, to save money.
- Take an on-demand backup before every schema migration.
- Firestore: model documents around how the page **reads** them. Keep hot counters in their own small documents.
- Choose locations carefully. The Firestore location cannot be changed, and moving Cloud SQL means a migration.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Symptom | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Using the IP address instead of the socket from Cloud Run | connection timeouts | `--add-cloudsql-instances` and `host=/cloudsql/<connection name>` |
| Service account lacks `roles/cloudsql.client` | `403` / `NOT_AUTHORIZED` in the logs | grant `roles/cloudsql.client` |
| Large pools on many instances | `FATAL: sorry, too many clients already` | shrink the pool or cap `--max-instances` (formula below) |
| `ZONAL` instance in prod | the shop is down during a zone outage | `--availability-type=REGIONAL` |
| Deleting the instance to "start fresh" | its automated backups are deleted with it | export first: `gcloud sql export sql …` |
| Reading a Firestore counter on every page view with high traffic | the free tier runs out by lunchtime | cache the value for a few seconds |

## Mathematical Abstraction

**Database connections** add up across all Cloud Run instances.

$$
n_{\max} \times k \le C_{\max}
$$

where:

- $n_{\max}$ is Cloud Run's `--max-instances`;
- $k$ is the pool size per instance (the `max` option in the code above);
- $n_{\max} \times k$ is the most connections the app can open at once;
- $C_{\max}$ is the database's connection limit (`SHOW max_connections;`), minus a few kept free for admins;
- $\le$ says the left side must not exceed the right side.

Example: $n_{\max} = 10$ and $k = 5$ give $10 \times 5 = 50$ connections. If $C_{\max} = 100$, then $50 \le 100$ holds, with room to spare. Remove `--max-instances` and a traffic spike could start 100 instances: $100 \times 5 = 500 > 100$, and new customers would get `too many clients`.

**How much data can you lose?** The worst case is the time since the last restore point.

$$
L_{\max} = \begin{cases}
\Delta_{\text{backup}} & \text{without point-in-time recovery} \\
\Delta_{\text{log}} & \text{with point-in-time recovery}
\end{cases}
$$

where:

- $L_{\max}$ is the largest amount of recent work, measured in time, that a restore could lose (the recovery point objective);
- $\Delta_{\text{backup}}$ is the time between automated backups;
- $\Delta_{\text{log}}$ is how far the archived write-ahead log lags behind the live database, usually seconds to a few minutes.

Example: with daily backups at 03:00 and no point-in-time recovery, $\Delta_{\text{backup}} = 24$ hours. A bad migration at 02:55 the next night loses up to $24\,\text{h} - 5\,\text{min} = 23\,\text{h}\,55\,\text{min}$ of orders. With point-in-time recovery, you restore to 02:54 and lose only the last minute or so.

**Will Firestore stay free?** Daily reads are visits times reads per visit.

$$
R = v \times r \le 50{,}000
$$

where:

- $v$ is the number of page views per day;
- $r$ is the number of documents each page view reads;
- $R$ is the total reads per day;
- $50{,}000$ is the Standard edition's free daily read allowance (at the time of writing).

Example: the menu page reads 2 documents (today's counter and the specials), so $r = 2$. With $v = 12{,}000$ views, $R = 12{,}000 \times 2 = 24{,}000 \le 50{,}000$: free. On a festival day, $v = 30{,}000$ gives $R = 60{,}000$, which is $10{,}000$ reads over. Caching the counter for 10 seconds would bring it back under.
